title: Author Correction: Epigenetic priming of mammalian embryonic enhancer elements coordinates developmental gene networks
ERVmancer: a phylogeny-guided framework for decoding human endogenous retrovirus regulatory mechanisms in health and disease
abstract: Human endogenous retroviruses (HERVs) are remmants of ancient infections which make up to ~8% of the human genome. Their activity influences development, immunity, and cancer, but studying them has been limited by a key technical challenge: short-read sequencing cannot uniquely assign reads to these highly repetitive elements. Here, we present ERVmancer, a phylogeny-informed method that resolves the read-mapping ambiguity and quantifies HERV expression across scales, from individual loci to entire retroviral clades, depending on mapping confidence. Benchmarking with sample-matched long- and short-read data generated in this study demonsrates that ERVmancer outperforms existing approaches in both sensitivity and specificity. Application of ERVmancer recapitulates known HERV expression patterns in multiple sclerosis and uncovers new biology in breast cancer, including suppression of HERVH-LTR7 by p53. By enabling accurate and scalable quantification of integrated retroviral elements, ERVmancer provides a broadly applicable resource for investigating retroviral mechanisms in health and disease.

title: Spatial and single-nucleus transcriptomics reveal the complexity of genomic imprinting in maize
abstract: Abstract Genomic imprinting is a classical epigenetic phenomenon first discovered in maize, which occurs almost exclusively in the triploid endosperm and is thought to mediate parental conflicts over offspring survival. Although previous studies using manually dissected maize endosperm from reciprocal hybrids coupled with RNA sequencing have uncovered hundreds of putative imprinted genes, the intensive cellular heterogeneity within endosperm has been overlooked, leaving it unclear whether imprinting varies across different cell types. Here, we applied 10x spatial transcriptomics and single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) to profile reciprocal maize kernels, resolving six major endosperm cell types. We reveal a high degree of cell-type specificity of allele-specific expression (ASE) genes that approximately two-thirds of them occurring in a single endosperm cell type. Additionally, over 70% of imprinted genes identified by spatial transcriptomics can be validated by snRNA-seq at the cell-type level. Fewer than half of them are found in multiple endosperm cell types, and paternally expressed genes (PEGs) outnumber maternally expressed genes (MEGs) by approximately two-fold. We disclosed an imprinted long non-coding RNA (lncRNA) that clustered with the typical MEG Mez1 in a maternally hypomethylated region. Our findings provide fresh evidence that post-fertilization endosperm differentiation may shape the spatial and cellular complexity of genomic imprinting in maize.

title: Landscape and mutational dynamics of G-quadruplexes across the complete human genome
abstract: Abstract Background G-quadruplexes (G4s) are alternative DNA structures with diverse biological roles, but their examination in highly repetitive parts of the human genome has been hindered by the lack of reliable sequencing technologies. Recent long-read based genome assemblies have enabled their characterization in previously inaccessible parts of the human genome. Here, we examine the topography and genomic instability of potential G4-forming sequences in the gap-less, reference human genome assembly and in 88 haplotypes of diverse ancestry. Results We report that G4s are highly enriched in specific repetitive regions, including in certain centromeric and pericentromeric repeat types, and in ribosomal DNA arrays, and experimentally validate the most prevalent G4s detected. G4s tend to have lower methylation than expected and are genomically unstable, showing an excess of insertions and deletions. Finally, we show that G4-forming motifs are consistently enriched at meiotic DSB hotspots across individuals with different PRDM9 genotypes. Conclusions Together, our findings establish G4s as dynamic and functionally significant elements of the human genome and highlight new avenues for investigating their contributions to human disease and evolution.

title: Autumn–winter progression triggers distinct transcriptional programs in Arabidopsis thaliana
abstract: Abstract Background Temperate plants are adapted to survive winter chilling temperatures. However, the global regulatory landscape underlying acclimation to noisy and fluctuating natural cold conditions remains poorly investigated. Results We explore the transcriptome dynamics of Arabidopsis thaliana plants grown over weeks of a gradually decreasing temperature regime, mimicking natural cold conditions of autumn and early winter, including daily temperature fluctuations. Our results define two distinct genetic programs responding to either moderate cold ( COOLING genes) or to temperatures below 10 °C ( CHILLING genes). Transient induction of C-REPEAT/DEHYDRATION-RESPONSIVE ELEMENT BINDING FACTORS ( CBFs ) lies in the boundary between COOLING and CHILLING activation, while the core circadian clock component CIRCADIAN CLOCK-ASSOCIATED 1 ( CCA1 ) is essential for transcriptional responses both at moderate cold and chilling conditions. By profiling genome-wide chromatin accessibility, we demonstrate that the induction of cold-responsive genes is associated with an increase in promoter accessibility. In contrast, down-regulated genes do not lose promoter accessibility, allowing plants to rapidly reactivate transcription after the return to warm conditions. Conclusions Overall, our work provides a comprehensive view of the extent of transcriptome and promoter accessibility dynamics underlying plant adaptation to cooling and chilling conditions, revealing the function of key regulators at specific low temperature ranges.

title: Transforming antibiotic tolerance research through genomics
abstract: Abstract Antibiotic tolerance is an increasingly recognised contributor to treatment failure. Integrating genomics with laboratory evolution and functional screening has shifted emphasis from studying tolerance as a transient, non-heritable phenotype to recognising its genetic underpinnings. These approaches reveal pathways that shape antibiotic survival beyond dormant-cell models. However, most insights derive from laboratory systems, leaving their clinical relevance unresolved. In this review, we discuss advances in genome-wide analyses of tolerance and their potential to identify candidate genes and variants in patient-derived isolates, resolve genetic architecture and epistasis, and uncover influences on resistance evolution, ultimately advancing the development of diagnostic and therapeutic strategies.

title: A curated genome-scale nucleotide diversity panel of non-human primates
abstract: BACKGROUND: Primates constitute one of the most phylogenetically and ecologically diverse eutherian mammalian orders and have a central role in advancing our knowledge of human evolution, speciation processes, and conservation biology. Although thousands of whole-genome sequences are available across many primate taxa, discrepancies in data processing-particularly the lack of ploidy-aware variant calling in sex-linked regions-have limited the utility of existing datasets for large-scale comparative analyses. RESULTS: Here, we use publicly available short-read sequencing data from non-human primates, recently published primate genome assemblies, and a ploidy-aware variant calling procedure to generate a genome-scale nucleotide diversity panel comprising 3,240 individuals from 269 species and 71 genera. To further facilitate cross-species comparisons, we generate a multiple-genome alignment of the primate assemblies used for variant calling. CONCLUSIONS: This curated resource of non-human primate diversity provides a foundation for future research in primate evolutionary biology, speciation, and sex chromosome evolution.

title: Integrating physiological and proteomics signatures for understanding drought, salinity and alkalinity stress tolerance mechanisms in lentil
abstract: Abiotic stresses—such as drought, salinity, and alkalinity severely limit global lentil production by impairing physiological processes including osmolytes accumulation, chlorophyll synthesis, H 2 O 2 production and antioxidant activities. However, no proteomic signature studies have dissected the molecular mechanisms underlying tolerance to drought, salinity and alkalinity in lentil. In this study, proteomic profiling revealed differentially abundant proteins (DAPs) distinguishing tolerant from sensitive lines under multiple abiotic stress conditions including drought, salinity and alkalinity. Furthermore, the aforementioned physiological traits were phenotyped to compare the responses of tolerant versus sensitive genotypes toward these stresses. By integrating proteomics and physiological analyses, this study provides new insights into the physiological and molecular regulatory mechanisms of lentil in response to multiple abiotic stresses. Physiological analysis revealed genotypic differences in osmolyte regulation, chlorophyll content, H 2 O 2 production and antioxidant activities. Ultra performance liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectrometery (UPLC-MS/MS) analysis identified 707 differentially abundant proteins (DAPs) between tolerant v/s sensitive genotypes across stresses, with 283, 213 and 211 DAPs under drought, salinity and alkalinity, respectively. Ninety-five DAPs involved in protein biogenesis, cellular transport, photosynthesis, RNA regulation, defense and detoxification were common across stresses. Proteomic findings were validated by quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR) of five DAPs at 1, 2 and 3 days post-stress. Functional annotation revealed enrichment in photosynthesis/energy metabolism, transcription/translational, protein folding/degradation, and antioxidative defense. Integrative transcriptomic and proteomic analysis highlighted superoxide dismutase and monodehydroascorbate reductase as central components of antioxidative defense. This represents the first proteomics study of lentil seedling response toward drought, salinity and alkalinity stresses. The differential abundance of proteins involved in varied regulatory pathways suggests a wide, yet complex network of proteins mediating lentil’s metabolic adaptation to drought, salinity and alkalinity stresses. Proteins identified in this study will provide new insight to lentil’s interconnected regulatory mechanisms against abiotic stresses.

title: Identification of regulators of aryl hydrocarbon receptor signaling in human cells by genome-scale CRISPR screening
abstract: Abstract Background The human aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AHR) integrates chemical signals derived from the environment, gut microbes, and endogenous sources to regulate processes ranging from intestinal barrier integrity to xenobiotic detoxification. Despite strong evidence that dysregulation of AHR signaling is a causal factor in metabolic and autoimmune disorders, we currently lack a comprehensive understanding of the factors that regulate AHR activity in human cells. Results Here, we use genome-scale CRISPR screening to systematically identify regulators of AHR signaling in a model of human hepatocytes. The resulting datasets recapitulate the core AHR signaling pathway and identify a large network of regulators. Many of these factors have roles beyond AHR signaling, reflecting that AHR signaling is deeply integrated into human cell biology. We further dissect this network to reveal novel modes of regulation of AHR expression, protein levels, and signaling. For example, we find that the E3 ubiquitin ligase UBR5 sustains AHR signaling by counteracting degradation of ligand-bound AHR. Finally, we identify components of the AHR regulatory network that are specific to cell types and ligands as potential nodes to manipulate AHR signaling in a targeted manner for therapeutic benefit. Conclusions Overall, our results define the regulatory network that underpins AHR activation, with implications for our understanding of host-microbe interactions and integrative chemosensation and the etiology of metabolic and inflammatory disorders.

title: TurbOmics: a web-based platform for the analysis of metabolomics data using a multi-omics integrative approach
abstract: ABSTRACT In recent years, multi-omics integration has proven highly effective for the holistic characterization of biological systems, with the development of numerous bioinformatic platforms. However, these tools face limitations when incorporating metabolomics data, including absence of support for untargeted metabolomics annotation and dependence on predefined knowledge bases. Furthermore, the advanced algorithms required for multi-omics integration typically demand programming skills and statistical background, restricting their use to specialized users. To advance towards resolving these challenges, we present TurbOmics, a user-friendly web-based platform that enables researchers with diverse backgrounds to analyze metabolomics, proteomics, and transcriptomics data using advanced algorithms for multi-omics integration, while addressing key challenges associated with metabolomics data. Users can upload quantitative data and include additional information, such as metabolite identification or lipid classes, that streamline the interpretation of complex results. TurbOmics can be used sequentially with our previously published tool, TurboPutative, to simplify, reduce and prioritize the list of putative annotations from untargeted metabolomics datasets. Thanks to its flexible and interactive interface, researchers can perform exploratory data analysis and multi-omics integration using the Multi-Omics Factor Analysis, Pathway Integrative Analysis and Enrichment Analysis modules. We believe that TurbOmics will make multi-omics analysis more accessible to the research community. The platform is freely available at https://proteomics.cnic.es/TurboPutative/TurbOmicsApp.html . Abstract Figure GRAPHICAL ABSTRACT

title: Surface proteomics reveals arginine metabolism as a vulnerability in high grade serous ovarian cancer
abstract: ABSTRACT Background The significant lethality of high-grade serous ovarian cancer (HGSC) is driven by the lack of long-term efficacy of current treatments, underscoring the need for developing additional therapeutics. Cell surface proteins represent attractive therapeutic targets yet remain underexplored in high-grade serous ovarian cancer. Here, we employed cell surface N -glycoproteomics to elucidate the cell surface proteomes of HGSC cells alongside normal epithelial and cancer-associated stromal cells, uncovering new opportunities for therapeutic intervention. Results Integration of cell surface N -glycoproteomics and functional screening revealed multiple minimally characterized, HGSC-enriched surface proteins that are critical for HGSC proliferation – most notably, SLC7A1. Multi-omic and functional characterization indicated that SLC7A1 is necessary for HGSC migration, protein synthesis and mitochondrial functions likely linked to its role as an arginine transporter. Finally, we demonstrate that elevated surface expression of SLC7A1 in HGSC reflects dysregulated arginine metabolism, pointing to a putative therapeutic vulnerability. Conclusions Our work identifies SLC7A1 and arginine metabolism as a previously unrecognized molecular vulnerability in HGSC and provides a framework to guide future therapeutic development.

title: Hi-C derived insulation strength predicts evolutionary conservation of topologically associating domains
abstract: Topologically associating domains (TADs) are fundamental units of three-dimensional chromatin organization, yet their functional significance and evolutionary conservation remain debated. We generate bulk Hi-C contact maps from the ventral hippocampus of eight inbred mouse strains, including five classical laboratory strains and three wild-derived strains, comprising 14.55 billion valid contacts. We show that discrete TAD and loop calling yields poor inter-replicate concordance, whereas separation scores, a continuous measure of boundary insulation strength, substantially improve reproducibility. Using this approach, we identify 2,857 highly insulated genomic regions whose insulation is conserved across all strains. These regions are enriched for multiple CTCF binding sites, accessible chromatin, and proximity to super-enhancers and housekeeping genes, and show greater DNA sequence conservation across placental mammals and more stable DNA methylation than expected by chance. Cross-species analysis reveals that the positional overlap of insulated regions between human and mouse increases with insulation strength, reaching 80.7% for the most highly insulated regions. While genomic structural rearrangements are the primary driver of chromatin conformation differences between strains, we find limited evidence that these differences have functional consequences. Together, these findings show that insulation strength tracks the evolutionary conservation of chromatin domain boundaries and correlates with features associated with functional importance, providing a quantitative framework for prioritizing candidate functionally critical TAD boundaries.

title: Poison exon splicing in the human brain provides a new paradigm for understanding and targeting neurological disorders
abstract: Abstract Background Poison exons (PE) are highly conserved exons whose inclusion creates premature termination codons (PTCs) and triggers nonsense-mediated decay (NMD) of the mature transcript. Despite their important role in post-transcriptional regulation, PEs remain poorly annotated due to the lack of systematic transcriptome-wide approaches. Results A comparative analysis of 957 eukaryotic transcriptomes revealed that Homo Sapiens exhibits the highest enrichment of NMD-targeted isoforms. By systematically predicting and annotating splicing events that generate PTCs, we found 9,814 PEs in the human genome. Using RNA-seq dataset from GTEx and BrainSpan, we analyzed PE splicing across tissues and developmental stages and identified 83 PEs uniquely found in the human brain, 973 PEs with brain-specific differential splicing, and 1,284 PEs differentially spliced during brain development. By integrating ClinVar variant annotations with SpliceAI predictions, we identified 1,625 pathogenic variants associated with neurological disorders that are predicted to affect the splicing of 743 PEs, and we functionally validated the impact of a subset of them using CRISPR prime-editing in human cells. Functional characterization of the deep intronic NDUFAF6 c.420+784C>T variant associated with Leigh syndrome demonstrated increased PE inclusion and a significant reduction in NDUFAF6 protein levels in iPSC-derived induced neurons. Mutant cells also exhibited impaired mitochondrial membrane potential compared to controls. Together, these findings provide functional evidence that the c.420+784C>T variant promotes aberrant PE inclusion, leading to reduced NDUFAF6 expression and mitochondrial dysfunction. Conclusions Our findings highlight PEs as pivotal regulators of gene expression in the human brain and support the therapeutic targeting of PE splicing in neurological diseases.

title: Pep2Net: an integrated peptide knowledge base and cross-attention model for multi-task prediction of peptides
abstract: Computational peptide design is hindered by fragmented databases and models separating semantic from physicochemical features. We introduce Pep2Net, a comprehensive platform addressing these issues. First, we develop Pep2Net-DB, unifying 52 peptide resources into an ontology-inspired knowledge base. Second, we develop Pep2Net-XAtt, a multi-task model leveraging cross-attention and low-rank bilinear pooling to fuse protein language model embeddings with physicochemical descriptors. Pep2Net-XAtt achieves state-of-the-art performance in predicting cell-penetrating, anticancer toxicity, and multi-functional peptides. Accessible via Pep2Net Web, this framework provides a unified tool for large-scale peptide characterization and design.

title: Germline structural variation involving gynecologic and breast cancers reveals polygenic signatures of tumor mutational load
abstract: Germline structural variants (SVs), genomic variants involving larger segments of the human genome, are understudied in the context of cancer. The impact of germline variants on the regulation of specific genes is highly dependent on tissue and cellular context, necessitating focused, multi-omics studies by cancer tissue of origin. Here, we combine patient germline SV data with tumor multi-omics profiling across 2006 breast and gynecologic cancers, including breast, cervical, ovarian, uterine endometrial, and uterine carcinosarcoma tumors, to determine the extent to which germline SV patterns influence the tumor molecular landscape. Rare germline SV events predicted to disrupt specific cancer-relevant genes cumulatively affect approximately 29% of patients. We find thousands of genes exhibit significant associations between nearby germline SV breakpoints and altered tumor gene expression or DNA methylation. These associations are either specific to tumor type or shared across multiple tumor types and involve numerous cancer-relevant genes. We also identify widespread associations of germline SV patterns with tumor somatic mutational load, including copy number alteration and somatic structural variation, with similar patterns observed in additional cancer cohorts beyond gynecologic and breast cancers. Notably, we find a germline deletion SV spanning UGT2B17 (involving 36% of patients), is associated with reduced UGT2B17 expression and lower tumor mutational load. Germline SV-associated dysregulation in known cancer susceptibility genes or established cancer related genes considerably expands the spectrum of patients with evidence of a germline contribution to cancer development or progression. The patient’s genetic background may influence tumor characteristics, including somatic mutational load.

title: TraSPIN: inferring transporter specificity through language model-guided graph learning
abstract: Abstract Membrane transporters orchestrate chemical exchange across cells, playing a central role in cellular metabolism and serving as prime targets for disease intervention. Yet, the specific substrates of most transport proteins remain unknown, largely because experimental characterization is hindered by the instability of membrane proteins in experimental assays. Existing computational tools are often limited to narrow substrate classes or fail to generalize to distant homologs. Here, we present TraSPIN, a geometric deep learning framework that jointly models paired representations of transporter proteins and small-molecule substrates. TraSPIN consistently outperforms existing predictors, demonstrating excellent generalization to both novel substrates and sequence-dissimilar transporters. The model moves beyond mere prediction to reveal the underlying structural mechanisms and motifs governing transporter-substrate recognition. Through large-scale inference across diverse species and successful de-orphanization of uncharacterized solute carrier proteins, we highlight TraSPIN’s broad applicability. This powerful framework establishes a robust foundation for deciphering membrane transport, with immediate implications for drug discovery and systems medicine.

title: Dynamic landscapes of gene regulatory networks during early mammalian neurogenesis for understanding brain evolution and disorder risk
abstract: Neurogenesis is governed by dynamic transcriptional programs that vary across developmental time, brain region, and cell type, thereby forming regionally specialized neuronal circuits. However, the gene regulatory networks (GRNs) that coordinate these processes across species and brain regions are still not fully characterized. To address this, we construct a comprehensive GRN resource encompassing 24 neurogenic lineages from human, macaque, and mouse, enabling systematic cross-species and cross-regional comparisons. Integrated analyses characterize temporal regulatory dynamics and introduce a dynamic score to identify lineage-specific regulatory subnetworks, revealing hundreds of dynamic regulons and co-regulatory modules. We identify both known and novel candidate regulators that underlie neuronal differentiation and regional identity across the human brain and uncovered evolutionary divergence in neurogenic GRNs that distinguishes neurogenesis in humans from other species. Experimental characterization of the candidate neurogenic regulator ILF2 provides evidence for its role in neurogenesis. Furthermore, mapping disease-associated genes onto this resource reveals gene regulatory dynamics linked to 30 neurological disorders and traits, including autism spectrum disorder, schizophrenia, intellectual disability, and microcephaly. Our study provides a comprehensive cross-species and cross-regional atlas of neurogenic gene regulatory networks and their temporal dynamics. This resource facilitates the discovery of key regulators of early neuronal development, offers insights into the evolution of human brain regulatory programs, and enables the investigation of disease-associated regulatory mechanisms. The resource is freely accessible through an interactive online platform.

title: The contribution of short tandem repeats to splicing variation in the human prefrontal cortex
abstract: Abstract Background Splicing disruption has been implicated in a range of heritable phenotypes, including numerous psychiatric and neurological disorders. Recent studies have focused largely on single nucleotide polymorphisms or short indels. Despite growing evidence that genetic variation at short tandem repeats (STRs) influences splicing, large-scale studies of STR-mediated splicing in the brain have been limited by low sample sizes of available RNA-seq data or exclusion of certain classes of STRs. Results Here, we leverage deep RNA-seq and SNP array data from 336 human dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) samples collected by the Human Brain Collection Core. We identify 51,343 unique STRs for which copy number is significantly associated with one or multiple alternative splicing events of nearby genes (spliceSTRs). We prioritize and characterize candidate causal spliceSTRs using three orthogonal fine-mapping strategies, identifying 1,313 high-confidence fine-mapped spliceSTRs, and further find strong associations between copy number of certain repeat units and binding of specific RNA-binding proteins (RBPs). Co-localization analyses using summary statistics from genome-wide association studies for 6 brain-related disorders identified multiple signals that may be driven by fine-mapped spliceSTRs, including a previously identified ( GT ) n repeat that is a spliceSTR for PLEKHA1 associated with Alzheimer’s disease as well as a newly identified ( AGG ) n spliceSTR in SEPTIN3 co-localized with schizophrenia. Conclusions Our findings highlight the role of STRs in regulating alternative splicing in the human brain, suggesting a general relationship between STR polymorphism and RBP-mediated splicing events, and identify specific spliceSTRs detected by co-localization analysis as candidate causal variants for brain-related disorders.

title: Non-invasive genomic sampling uncovers novel connectivities and origins of confiscated gorillas
abstract: Abstract Background Gorillas are a group of African great apes with two species and four subspecies that are currently critically endangered or endangered. Previous studies analyzing the genetics of wild gorillas from non-invasive samples such as faeces or hair have analysed short mitochondrial or nuclear markers, which may not reflect the wider nuclear genome. Recent technical advances in target capture hybridisation, enrich the endogenous DNA content of non-invasive samples, allowing contiguous genomic regions to be sequenced. Results Here, we generate georeferenced genetic dataset from faecal and hair samples of 280 wild gorillas, sampled from three of the four gorilla subspecies, across large parts of their present-day distributions. With this expanded representation of gorilla genetic diversity in the wild, we detect three population clusters in western lowland gorillas, with the Sangha River and its affluents acting as significant barriers to gene flow. We reconstruct patterns of past population connectivity between western lowland gorillas in the north-eastern distribution range and Cross River gorillas, which may have been facilitated by a migration corridor also used by the Central and Nigeria-Cameroon chimpanzee subspecies. Finally, we predict the geographic origins of wild-born gorillas, achieving a mean prediction error of 65 km, with a population-level resolution for mountain gorillas and some populations of western lowland gorillas. Conclusion Our work characterises fine-scale population structure in western lowland gorillas, which will be informative for future conservation strategies. This proof-of-concept in predicting geographic locations of wild gorillas, will be useful for future applications to geolocalise trafficked or rescued gorillas.

title: A new phased assembly of the Antarctic spiny plunderfish provides novel insights into the evolution of the notothenioid radiation
abstract: Abstract Background Notothenioids are a well characterised species flock endemic to the Antarctic and an important model group for studying genome adaptation to extreme cold. A new reference assembly and clade-wide comparative genomic analysis allow for investigation of cryonotothenioid evolution and the appearance of novel functionalities linked to cold adaptation. Results A new phased assembly of a model notothenioid, Harpagifer antarcticus , demonstrated low levels of haplotypic variability across the genome. Nevertheless, numerous insertions from multiple LINE-L2 clades were found, suggesting ongoing transposition with potential contribution to speciation. Contrary to expectations the afgp locus was highly similar between haplotypes, except for large length allelic variants of afgp genes. Analysis suggests a model for the afgp locus expansion in H. antarcticus through segmental tandem duplications involving two pairs of afgp genes at time. Syntenic reconstruction of genomes from across the clade demonstrates conserved macrosyntenic relationships and group specific chromosomal fusions of notothenioids. Quantification of genome gain and transposition rates during cryonotothenioid diversification showed a first ancestral slow genome expansion concurrent with historic temperature drops. This was followed by lineage-specific massive peaks of genomic gain and transposition activity. Finally, we identified a set of genes that underwent ancestral diversifying selection and acquired novel conserved non-coding elements during the cryonotothenioid emergence. These were related to antioxidants and proteostasis, which may have facilitated the notothenioid Antarctic radiation. Conclusions Diversifying selection and genomic gain linked to transposon activity are primary contributors to lineage-specific evolutionary dynamics through the clade which facilitated adaptation to life in the cold.

title: Extensive admixture and introgression shape genetic diversity and evolutionary adaptation in indigenous East Asian cattle
abstract: The complex introgression history of indigenous East Asian cattle is at the root of their remarkable diversity. Characterization of this diversity is a crucial step in understanding the genomic basis of adaptation to East Asian agricultural systems. However, the evolutionary history of indigenous East Asian cattle has remained poorly documented. Here, we present the largest short-read whole-genome sequencing dataset to date, including 802 indigenous Chinese cattle of 55 breeds/populations from diverse geographic regions, to address the population structure, genetic origins, and biological adaptations of this underrepresented population. We identify seven distinct genetic populations within Chinese cattle that were influenced by inter- and intraspecific introgression. We review introgression from Asian bovine species and reveal its geographical distribution characteristics in Chinese cattle. We identify a major taurine × indicine cattle admixture event during the Tang and Song dynasties (894–1210 AD ), which facilitated rapid local adaptation with a predominant effect on the immune system. Moreover, we present a comprehensive catalog of loci that underwent divergent selection across East Asian agroecological zones, including genes associated with cold tolerance, heat tolerance and meat production. Our findings indicate that admixture between taurine and indicine cattle, together with introgression from other Asian bovine species, contributed to the adaptive evolution of indigenous East Asian cattle.

title: ROMET-RNA benchmarks and selects RNA 3D structures using multiple predictors and alignment strategies
abstract: Accurate prediction of RNA tertiary structure is essential for understanding RNA function, yet systematic, controlled benchmarking and integration of RNA three-dimensional structure prediction methods, particularly with respect to multiple sequence alignment strategies used by deep learning models, remain limited. Here, we present ROMET-RNA, an automated benchmarking framework and meta-selection toolkit that benchmarks eleven state-of-the-art RNA structure predictors within a standardized workflow and evaluates three complementary MSA pipelines, rMSA, RNAcmap3 MARS, and Infernal RNAcentral. Model selection is performed using a consensus scoring strategy combining TM-scoreRNA based structural similarity with the deep learning derived statistical potential lociPARSE. Benchmarking across four non-redundant test sets comprising 205 RNAs, including CASP15, RNA Puzzles, and recent PDB structures, demonstrates that ROMET-RNA consistently selects more accurate models than individual methods would on its own and we confirm that this is not an artefact of training-test overlap. Further analysis reveals that coevolutionary information substantially improves accuracy, that optimal MSA strategies are method specific, and that MSA depth exhibits a nonlinear relationship with performance. ROMET-RNA provides an open-source standardized framework that enhances RNA 3D structure model selection, supporting advances in RNA structural biology and genomics.

Amira: detection of single and multi-copy antimicrobial resistance genes directly from long reads using gene-space de Bruijn graphs
abstract: Abstract Accurate detection of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) genes is essential for AMR surveillance and genotypic prediction. Current approaches typically either depend on a correct genome assembly or use k-mers directly from the reads. However AMR genes are often multicopy and are enriched at repeat loci where genome assemblers tend to fail, and k-mer methods struggle to distinguish different copies. We present Amira, which detects AMR genes directly from long reads by building gene-space de Bruijn graphs, allowing precise association of reads with distinct AMR gene copies, enabling accurate assembly. Across simulations, curated samples, and public datasets, Amira improves copy-number recall and nucleotide accuracy compared with existing methods.

title: MineGraph facilitates plastid and mitochondrial graph pangenome analysis in plants
BioSIFTR: functional inference from shallow shotgun sequencing using biome-specific genome catalogues benchmarked in gut microbiomes
abstract: Abstract Shallow shotgun sequencing is an accurate microbiome profiling method, but its use for functions is limited. BioSIFTR extrapolates shallow shotgun read mapping to precalculated pangenome functions in 15 MGnify biome-specific catalogues, which span host-associated and environmental microbiomes. We benchmarked BioSIFTR on synthetic communities and on three gut microbiomes — red junglefowl, mouse, and human — using matched deep shotgun and 16S rRNA metabarcoding data, outperforming similar approaches. Further validation will require matched benchmark datasets and is a priority for future work. BioSIFTR is thus a practical method for functional inference from cost-effective shallow shotgun sequencing, currently validated in gut microbiomes.

title: Urbanisation drives parallel genomic divergence across cities and bumble bee species
abstract: Abstract Background Urbanisation imposes pervasive environmental change, yet it remains unclear whether evolutionary responses to cities are largely idiosyncratic or whether similar selective pressures across cities repeatedly generate predictable genomic outcomes. Results Here, we analyse whole-genome data from 524 individuals of three widespread bumble bee species sampled across nine independent urban–rural pairs in Central Europe to test whether urban environments drive parallel evolutionary responses across cities and species. Genetic diversity responded idiosyncratically to urbanisation, with two species showing no detectable urban–rural differences and one species exhibiting reduced diversity in cities, consistent with species-specific ecological traits and habitat requirements. Despite weak population structure and high gene flow in all species, we detected consistent and replicated genomic divergence associated with urban environments. Genome–environment association analyses revealed parallel allele-frequency shifts at the same loci across independent cities for each species, while selective sweep scans identified repeated signals of positive selection in urban populations. Across species, urban-associated divergence was highly polygenic and occurred predominantly in non-coding regions with potential regulatory roles. Although the specific genes involved were largely species-specific, functional enrichment analyses revealed strong convergence across species, particularly in pathways related to physiological stress responses, neurocognitive and behavioural processes, metabolism and immunity. Conclusions Together, these results suggest that urban environments can impose recurrent selective pressures, generating predictable and parallel genomic responses across cities and species despite ongoing gene flow. More broadly, our findings highlight polygenic, potentially regulatory adaptation as an important component of evolutionary responses to urban environments.

title: Mitonuclear control of transcription complexes regulates tRNA splicing

The glutamine-aspartate metabolic tradeoff between fast growth and metabolic flexibility
abstract: Abstract Background Cancer cells develop selective dependencies on nutrients, creating potential opportunities for therapeutic intervention. However, how metabolic rewiring enables cancer cells to sustain proliferation while adapting to nutrient limitation remains incompletely understood. Results We develop a systematic framework to investigate nutrient dependencies and apply it to extracellular glutamine dependence. By measuring metabolite exchange rates across 54 cancer cell lines with different degrees of glutamine dependence, together with metabolic profiling of human stem-cell differentiation, we identify tissue-associated differences in the use of glutamine and aspartate for glutamate biosynthesis. These differences are linked to a trade-off between rapid proliferation and metabolic flexibility. Time-resolved intracellular metabolomics following glutamine withdrawal reveal a common limitation in purine biosynthesis. However, this metabolic limitation alone is insufficient to explain glutamine dependency, suggesting that additional regulatory responses to glutamine deprivation contribute to growth arrest. Conclusions Our study provides a systematic framework for identifying metabolic features associated with nutrient dependence and shows how established functions of glutamine, aspartate and asparagine are coordinated across diverse cancer cell types. This approach may support the mechanistic characterization and pharmacological targeting of metabolic dependencies beyond glutamine addiction.

title: Mitigating bias in spatial transcriptomic pipelines via human feedback with CSDE
abstract: Abstract Biological discovery from large-scale assays requires extensive preprocessing, during which raw outputs (e.g., images, sequences) are processed into structured forms amenable to analysis. In spatial transcriptomics, differential expression analysis depends on cell segmentation, gene expression quantification, and cell-type annotation, all prone to systematic errors. We introduce corrected spatial differential expression (CSDE), building on prediction-powered inference to leverage a small set of expert-validated cells to correct for preprocessing bias. Across three case studies, CSDE yields more reliable differential expression estimates than the prevalent approach neglecting preprocessing.

title: Chemogenomic profiling of diverse Saccharomyces cerevisiae strains using the novel CRISPR-Cas9 markerless barcoded library BarMix
Telomere-to-telomere genome of a dodecaploid desert shrub Prunus pedunculata reveals polyploidy-driven arid adaptation
abstract: Abstract Background Geographical imbalance in extremophile plant genomics has left the Mongolian Plateau underexplored. Prunus pedunculata , a desert shrub endemic to this arid region, provides an ideal system for understanding woody plant adaptation to extreme drought, yet its genomic architecture remains unknown. Results Here we present a telomere-to-telomere genome assembly for P. pedunculata , a dodecaploid (2n = 12 × = 96) with the highest ploidy level among sequenced woody perennials. Its 1.38 Gb genome is resolved into 48 chromosomes, and telomeric repeats are detected in each. Evolutionary analysis confirms an autopolyploid origin with > 80% subgenome consistency and no evidence of hybridization. The most recent whole-genome duplication dates to approximately 3.49 million years ago, coinciding with the uplift of the Tibetan Plateau and the intensification of Asian interior aridity. Ancestral karyotype reconstruction using six Prunus species spanning diploid to dodecaploid genomes and three inflorescence types reveals an eight chromosome ancestor and post polyploidization chromosomal rearrangements. Organ specific transcriptomics under progressive drought uncovers a coordinated division of labor that integrates ABA, CLE25 , BES1 / BIN2 , and auxin signaling modules to orchestrate growth cessation and stress survival. Drought induced genes significantly overlap with expanded gene families, demonstrating functional recruitment of polyploidy derived redundancy. Conclusions This work confirms an autopolyploid origin for P. pedunculata and links this polyploidization event to the aridification of the Asian interior. Duplicated genes have been repurposed for drought stress, and a multi-component signaling network coordinates organ responses and enhances survival under water scarcity, offering leads for crop improvement.

title: CellPatch: a flexible and efficient framework for single-cell foundation models empowered by heuristic gene patching
abstract: Abstract Foundation models have advanced single-cell omics analysis but often remain too complex for practical use. We present CellPatch, a lightweight foundation model combining cross-attention with heuristic gene patching to reduce computational complexity during pretraining and fine-tuning while enabling inspection of gene-attention patterns. Across single-cell RNA-sequencing datasets spanning multiple organs and tissue states, CellPatch achieves state-of-the-art performance on diverse prediction tasks. Its modular design supports linear, adapter-based and task-specific architectures, enabling CellPatch to be adapted to diverse biological tasks.
